newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Nearly 2.5 million Bangladeshis hit by cyclone.
newsitem.headline: Nearly 2.5 million Bangladeshis hit by cyclone.

text.p: Nearly 2.5 million people were affected by a cyclone in Bangladesh that is feared to have killed more than 100 and the government said on Wednesday medical squads were trying to prevent outbreaks of disease in devastated areas.

"There is no report of spreading of diseases in the affected areas, but the government has taken every precaution. Some 622 medical teams are now working in the affected places," Jawadul Karim, press secretary to Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, told reporters.
He put the official death toll so far from Monday's cyclone at 95 -- down from the 121 earlier reported by police and officials.
However, officials, police and the Cyclone Preparedness Centre (CPC) in Chittagong said the death toll might still rise, with some 1,500 fishermen still unaccounted for in the Bay of Bengal.
"Many of them may not return," one official in Cox's Bazar said.
"The death count may go up but we don't expect any dramatic rise," one CPC official said.
Newspapers said the cyclone had killed between 350 and 500 people, and at least 5,000 were injured.
Karim said Hasina on Wednesday flew to the affected areas for a second day, supervising relief work in the islands of St. Martin's, Swandip and Bashkhali and other badly hit areas.

Karim said foreign diplomats and representatives of the European Union, the U.S aid agency USAID, the U.N. Development Programme (UNDP) and the International Committee of the Red Cross visited the worst hit Cox's Bazar districts and two islands on Wednesday.
Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad is due to brief diplomats on the effects of the cyclone, but Karim declined to say if Bangladesh would seek any foreign assistance.
Aid agency officials said the cyclone survivors needed immediate help, especially in rebuilding their homes.
"The immediate need is house building materials for the victims, prices of which have gone up by over 50 percent," said Gawhar Nayeem of Oxfam.
Low-lying Bangladesh is prone to devastation from cyclones. The country's worst storm in 1991 killed at least 138,000 people and left millions homeless.
Officials on Tuesday night said nearly 400,000 houses had been damaged and 15,000 cattle killed.
"We are making a full assessment of the losses, which may take a week or more. But so far it looks like that the extent (of damage) is within a manageable limit," an official said.
Nayeem, who has worked for Oxfam since before the 1991 cyclone, said this year's "minimal loss of life and property" was due to several reasons.
"The first was that storm warning and evacuation of likely victims came well in advance. The number of shelters was more than in 1991 and people had enough time to prepare themselves."
Agriculture officials said the country's rice crop largely escaped damage.
